content: Willows, sallows, and osiers belong to the genus Salix, which comprises approximately 400 species of deciduous trees and shrubs. These plants are predominantly found in moist soils within cold and temperate regions of the Northern Hemisphere. Most species are commonly referred to as willows, but certain narrow-leaved shrub species are called osiers, while some broader-leaved species are known as sallows. The term sallow is derived from the Latin word salix, meaning willow. Some willow species, particularly those adapted to arctic and alpine environments, grow as low-lying or creeping shrubs. For instance, the dwarf willow (Salix herbacea) rarely grows taller than 6 cm, although it spreads extensively across the ground. Willows are highly cross-fertile, and numerous hybrids occur both naturally and through cultivation. A notable example is the weeping willow (Salix × sepulcralis), a widely planted ornamental tree that is a hybrid between the Chinese Peking willow and the European white willow. The leaves and bark of the willow tree have been recognized for their medicinal properties since ancient times. Historical records from Assyria, Sumer, and Egypt describe their use as remedies for pain and fever. The Ancient Greek physician Hippocrates also documented the therapeutic benefits of willow in the 5th century BCE. Indigenous peoples of the Americas extensively utilized willow as a cornerstone of their traditional medicine. The medicinal efficacy of willow is attributed to its content of salicylic acid, a natural precursor to aspirin. In 1763, Reverend Edward Stone in England observed the medicinal properties of willow bark and reported his findings to the Royal Society, which subsequently published them. The active compound in willow bark, salicin, was first isolated in its crystalline form in 1828 by Henri Leroux, a French pharmacist, and Raffaele Piria, an Italian chemist. Piria further succeeded in purifying salicin into its acidic form, which was named salicylic acid due to its acidic nature in water (pH = 2.4). In 1897, Felix Hoffmann, a chemist working for Bayer AG, synthesized a modified version of salicylic acid derived from the Spiraea plant. This new compound, acetylsalicylic acid, caused less gastrointestinal irritation compared to pure salicylic acid. Hoffmann's creation was named aspirin, marking the advent of a groundbreaking class of medications known as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs).
